newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: AUA sees big savings from Lauda link-up.
newsitem.headline: AUA sees big savings from Lauda link-up.

text.p: Austrian Airlines (AUA), fresh from gaining a 36 percent stake in Lauda Air and an option to buy an additional 30 percent, forecast the deal would bring up to 300 million schillings ($25 million) in savings annually.
"For AUA the synergy effects will be worth up to 200 million schillings a year and Lauda is talking about up to 100 million schillings," AUA director Mario Rehulka told reporters.
Savings would be exclusively in the back office and handling operations, Rehulka said, underlining earlier statements that there would be no change to the service offered to passengers.
"Each airline has its own image. It would be wrong to blur the distinction," he said.
The firms announced last week that AUA would take a 36 percent stake in Lauda and had acquired an option to buy founder Niki Lauda's remaining 30 percent of shares at a fixed price by the year 2022.
The deal is subject to regulatory clearance.
At the same time German flag carrier Lufthansa said it was cutting its stake in Lauda Air to 20 percent from 39.7 percent and selling the 19.7 percent holding to AUA.

Financial details of the agreement have yet to emerge. AUA director Herbert Bammer declined to comment on a media report that the airline had paid 160 million schillings for the entire share package, with 50 million going directly to Niki Lauda.
AUA, Lauda and Tyrolean, which is 42.85 percent owned by AUA, have combined sales of about 20 billion schillings and carry some 6.2 million passengers to more than 100 destinations on 77 aircraft.

According to the terms of the agreement, AUA will continue to concentrate on scheduled flights, while Lauda will retain its traditional niche as a charter carrier. Tyrolean will continue to concentrate on regional traffic.
"The arrangement with Tyrolean has worked out very well. We will approach Lauda in the same way," Bammer said.
AUA stressed it had no plans to pour money into Lauda. Both firms would take responsibility for their own financial performance, Rehulka said.
He also dismissed speculation that Lufthansa may take a stake in AUA. "Lufthansa's strategy is geared towards coooperation not capital involvement," he said.

The Lauda board would remain unchanged despite the new ownership structure, AUA said. Bammer, Rehulka and AUA supervisory board president Rudolf Streicher expected to take up seats on Lauda's supervisory board. -- Vienna newsroom, +43-1 531 12 254 ($ = 11.90 Austrian Schillings)
